Political institutions also keep evolving in ways a static model output cannot fully track, which further favors retaining human-directed analysis. The rating rises to Medium, held there by the mandate and the residual verification core.

A decade out, AI will be a fluent, widely used explainer of government structure and constitutional doctrine, and the pure information-transmission rationale for the course is substantially eroded. But the GT-Pathways transfer mandate persists in the central case absent statewide policy change, and constitutional interpretation retains real verification burden — a citizen or practitioner relying on a confidently wrong institutional reading bears genuine cost. The rating holds Medium, capped by the general-education mandate and the residual critical-reasoning core from reaching High. The honest uncertainty concerns how the course is taught and assessed once AI produces competent civics analysis on demand, not whether foundational institutional literacy and the transfer requirement remain instrumentally in force — in the central case, both persist through 2036, anchored by the same GT-SS1 lock that holds the rating today.

PSC 2090.d: In this course students examine sociological concepts and historical themes as part of exploring the origins and nature of the Black Lives Matter (BLM) movement. In addition to high-profile incidences of police brutality, attention is given to movement dynamics as shaped by Internet social media platforms and cable news. Students will also analyze the #SayHerName movement, which has highlighted police violence against black women. Issues concerning misogynoir are also covered, including black radical feminist critiques of black male patriarchy, and debates within the black community about the movement's focus. Finally, students will come away with a broad understanding of what systemic institutionalized racism is, as distinguished from incidences of racial violence by individual acts of terrorism or white supremacist terrorist organizations.

PSC 2400.d: Students explore United States foreign policies in Africa since the post-1945 period to the present. For many, Africa was an unlikely place for the United States to begin to define its international role in a post-Cold War world. But as a continent where East-West tensions were often played out in the 1960s-1980s, there is a certain logic that it was also the continent where the U.S. foreign policy-making machinery was tested in the early days of a new world order. In this course students survey and analyze American foreign policies on the importance of Africa's resources, strategic position and challenges of development. It relates U.S. interests to the domestic political processes that shape its policies in Africa. This course thus addresses the questions of U.S. interests in Africa, past, present, and future, and Washington's policy toward the African continent.
